steps.explanation:
A spinning coin is a flat circle turning in place. Its key poses are the two extremes: face on, and edge on.

In Frame 1 the coin faces you: a full circle with a ring stamped inside it and a white highlight on its left half.

![Frame 1](examples/frame-1.png) ![Frame 5](examples/frame-5.png)

In Frame 5 the coin is edge on: a strip 5 pixels wide, outline included. Nothing is left of the face. The shading still follows the light: pale at the top, darker below.

![Frame 1](examples/frame-1.png) ![Frame 5](examples/frame-5.png)

Frames 2 to 4 turn the coin from face on to edge on. Frame 2 is still 12 pixels wide, then the coin narrows to 10 and 8 pixels before the strip in Frame 5. As it turns, its far side shows as a band of darker orange down the right.

Turn on **Onion skin** (O) to see the Frames on either side.

![Frame 1](examples/frame-1.png) ![Frame 2](examples/frame-2.png) ![Frame 3](examples/frame-3.png)

Frame 3 is a little narrower than Frame 2, and the dark band down the right is a little wider.

![Frame 2](examples/frame-2.png) ![Frame 3](examples/frame-3.png) ![Frame 4](examples/frame-4.png)

Frame 4 is the last step before the edge: the face is now a thin oval.

![Frame 3](examples/frame-3.png) ![Frame 4](examples/frame-4.png) ![Frame 5](examples/frame-5.png)

Frames 6 to 8 turn the coin back to face on, and they are close to Frames 4, 3 and 2 flipped left to right. The light now catches the left edge instead, which is what shows the coin is still turning the same way and has not just bounced back.

![Frame 4](examples/frame-4.png) ![Frame 6](examples/frame-6.png)

Frame 8 matches Frame 2, flipped, and leads back into Frame 1. Press **Play preview** (P) to watch it spin. Reusing flipped Frames halves the drawing and keeps both halves of the turn even.

![Frame 2](examples/frame-2.png) ![Frame 8](examples/frame-8.png)
